object.working: Use VSEPR. SO₂ has three electron domains around S with one lone pair, giving bent molecular geometry. PH₃ has four electron domains around P with one lone pair, giving trigonal pyramidal geometry. CH₂O has carbon double bonded to O and single bonded to two H atoms: three electron domains and no lone pairs on carbon, so its electron and molecular geometry are both trigonal planar. SiH₄ has four bonding domains and no lone pairs, giving tetrahedral geometry.

We determine the molecular geometry of each species:
- SO₂: Sulfur has 6 valence electrons; it forms bonds with two oxygens and retains one lone pair (3 electron domains: 2 bonding, 1 lone pair), giving a bent geometry.
- PH₃: Phosphorus has 5 valence electrons; it forms three single bonds with hydrogen and has one lone pair (4 domains: 3 bonding, 1 lone pair), giving a trigonal pyramidal geometry.
- CH₂O: Carbon has 4 valence electrons; it forms two single bonds with hydrogen and a double bond with oxygen (3 bonding domains, 0 lone pairs), yielding a trigonal planar molecular geometry.
- SiH₄: Silicon forms four single bonds with hydrogen (4 bonding domains, 0 lone pairs), yielding a tetrahedral geometry.
Therefore, CH₂O is trigonal planar.

The nitrate ion (NO₃⁻) has a total of 5 + (3 × 6) + 1 = 24 valence electrons. In the Lewis structure, nitrogen is the central atom bonded to three oxygen atoms (one double bond and two single bonds in any given resonance form, with formal charges of +1 on N and -1 on two oxygens). Nitrogen has 3 electron domains and 0 lone pairs. According to VSEPR theory, a steric number of 3 with no lone pairs gives a trigonal planar electron-domain geometry and a trigonal planar molecular geometry with bond angles of 120°.

The nitrate ion has nitrogen as the central atom bonded to three oxygen atoms, with resonance structures involving one N=O and two N-O bonds. Nitrogen has no lone pair in the dominant Lewis structure, so there are three electron domains around nitrogen. Three electron domains with no lone pairs give a trigonal planar electron and molecular geometry.

Determine the molecular geometry for each species using VSEPR theory:
- ClF₃: Chlorine has 7 valence electrons, forms 3 single bonds with fluorine, and has 2 lone pairs (steric number 5). Its molecular geometry is T-shaped.
- CO₃²⁻: Carbon has 4 valence electrons + 2 from the negative charge = 6 valence electrons. It forms three bonds to oxygen atoms (with resonance giving equivalent 1.33 bond orders) and has 0 lone pairs on the central carbon (steric number 3). Its molecular geometry is trigonal planar with ideal 120° bond angles and three identical bonded atoms.
- SO₃²⁻: Sulfur has 6 valence electrons + 2 = 8 valence electrons, forming 3 bonds to oxygen with 1 lone pair (steric number 4). Its geometry is trigonal pyramidal.
- NO₂⁻: Steric number 3 with 1 lone pair; geometry is bent.

CO₃²⁻ has carbon as the central atom with three electron domains, all bonding to three equivalent oxygen atoms. Carbon has no lone pair, so VSEPR gives a trigonal planar molecular geometry with O–C–O bond angles of 120°. ClF₃ is T-shaped due to two lone pairs on Cl. SO₃²⁻ has a lone pair on S, making it trigonal pyramidal. NO₂⁻ has only two bonded oxygen atoms and a lone pair on N, giving a bent geometry.

The ionic character of a bond increases with the absolute difference in electronegativity (ΔEN) between the two bonded atoms:
- O–S: |3.44 - 2.58| = 0.86
- Na–Cl: |3.16 - 0.93| = 2.23
- N–Cl: |3.16 - 3.04| = 0.12
- H–Cl: |3.16 - 2.20| = 0.96

Na–Cl has the largest difference in electronegativity (2.23) and is therefore predicted to have the greatest ionic character.

Ionic character increases with electronegativity difference. Calculate differences: O–S = |3.44 - 2.58| = 0.86; Na–Cl = |0.93 - 3.16| = 2.23; N–Cl = |3.04 - 3.16| = 0.12; H–Cl = |2.20 - 3.16| = 0.96. The largest difference is 2.23 for Na–Cl, so it is predicted to have the greatest ionic character.

Ionic character of a bond increases as the absolute difference in electronegativity (ΔEN) between the bonded atoms increases. Using the given values:
ΔEN(P–H) = |2.19 - 2.20| = 0.01
ΔEN(S–Cl) = |2.58 - 3.16| = 0.58
ΔEN(Si–Cl) = |1.90 - 3.16| = 1.26
ΔEN(K–Br) = |0.82 - 2.96| = 2.14
Ranking in order of increasing ionic character gives P–H < S–Cl < Si–Cl < K–Br, which corresponds to choice A.

Ionic character increases with electronegativity difference. Using Pauling values: P–H: |2.19 − 2.20| = 0.01; S–Cl: |2.58 − 3.16| = 0.58; Si–Cl: |1.90 − 3.16| = 1.26; K–Br: |0.82 − 2.96| = 2.14. Increasing order by difference is P–H < S–Cl < Si–Cl < K–Br.

The ionic character of a bond increases with the difference in Pauling electronegativity (Δχ) between the bonded atoms:
- Li–I: |2.66 - 0.98| = 1.68
- Be–O: |3.44 - 1.57| = 1.87
- C–F: |3.98 - 2.55| = 1.43
- O–Cl: |3.44 - 3.16| = 0.28

The Be–O bond has the largest electronegativity difference (1.87), meaning it has the greatest ionic character.

Ionic character increases with Pauling electronegativity difference. Calculate ΔEN for each bond: Li–I = |0.98 - 2.66| = 1.68; Be–O = |1.57 - 3.44| = 1.87; C–F = |2.55 - 3.98| = 1.43; O–Cl = |3.44 - 3.16| = 0.28. The largest difference is 1.87 for Be–O, so it has the greatest ionic character.

Determine the number of valence electrons around the central atom in each species: A. HCN has carbon with a single bond to H and a triple bond to N (8 electrons). B. PCl₃ has phosphorus with three single bonds to Cl and one lone pair (8 electrons). C. BF₃ has boron with three single bonds to F (6 electrons). D. XeF₂ has xenon with two single bonds to F and three lone pairs, for a total of 10 valence electrons surrounding the central atom (> 8 electrons).

HCN has C with four bonding electrons (8 total). PCl₃ has P with three bonds and one lone pair, totaling 8 electrons. BF₃ has B with only 6 electrons, an incomplete octet. XeF₂ has Xe as the central atom with two Xe–F bonds and three lone pairs: 2(2) + 3(2) = 10 electrons around Xe, which is more than eight.

Total valence electrons for IF₅ = 7 (from I) + 5 × 7 (from F) = 42 valence electrons. Iodine forms 5 single bonds with the 5 fluorine atoms, using 5 × 2 = 10 electrons. Each fluorine atom completes its octet with 3 lone pairs (5 × 6 = 30 electrons). The remaining 42 - (10 + 30) = 2 electrons are placed as a lone pair on the central iodine atom. Thus, the central iodine atom is surrounded by 5 bonding pairs and 1 lone pair, totaling 6 electron pairs or 12 electrons.

IF5 has 42 valence electrons total (I has 7, each F has 7). The best Lewis structure has five I—F single bonds, using 10 bonding electrons. Each fluorine gets three lone pairs, using 6 electrons each for 30 electrons. This leaves 2 electrons as one lone pair on iodine. Therefore, the central iodine is surrounded by 10 bonding electrons + 2 lone-pair electrons = 12 electrons.

Count total valence electrons for each species:
- NO₃⁻: 5 + 3(6) + 1 = 24 electrons. N obeys the octet rule (8 electrons).
- PH₄⁺: 5 + 4(1) - 1 = 8 electrons. P forms 4 single bonds to H (8 electrons).
- ICl₂⁻: 7 + 2(7) + 1 = 22 electrons. Two I-Cl single bonds use 4 electrons, Cl octets use 12 electrons, leaving 6 electrons (3 lone pairs) to be placed on the central iodine atom. Iodine has 2 bonding pairs and 3 lone pairs, totaling 10 electrons (an expanded octet).
- BF₄⁻: 3 + 4(7) + 1 = 32 electrons. B forms 4 single bonds to F (8 electrons).

Thus, only ICl₂⁻ requires its central atom to have more than 8 electrons.

The formal charge is calculated using the formula: Formal Charge = V - N - B, where V is the number of valence electrons in the neutral free atom, N is the number of non-bonding electrons, and B is the number of covalent bonds. For oxygen, V = 6. The central oxygen atom has one lone pair (N = 2) and forms one double bond plus one single bond (B = 2 + 1 = 3 bonds). Therefore, Formal Charge = 6 - 2 - 3 = +1.

For ICl₂⁻, total valence electrons = 7 (I) + 2×7 (Cl) + 1 (charge) = 22. The best Lewis structure puts iodine as the central atom with two I–Cl single bonds and three lone pairs on iodine. Iodine therefore has 2×2 = 4 bonding electrons plus 6 lone-pair electrons = 10 electrons, exceeding an octet. The other choices have central atoms with only eight electrons: N in NO₃⁻ has resonance forms with four shared pairs, P in PH₄⁺ has four single bonds, and B in BF₄⁻ has four single bonds.

For the central oxygen: valence electrons = 6. It has one lone pair = 2 lone-pair electrons. It forms one double bond and one single bond, so bonding electrons = 4 + 2 = 6, and half of these = 3. Formal charge = valence - (lone-pair electrons + half bonding electrons) = 6 - (2 + 3) = +1.

Formal charge is calculated using the formula: Formal Charge = (valence electrons) − (non-bonding electrons) − (number of bonds). Nitrogen (Group 15) has 5 valence electrons. In the given structure, nitrogen forms one double bond and two single bonds (a total of 4 bonds) and has zero non-bonding electrons (no lone pairs). Therefore, Formal Charge = 5 − 0 − 4 = +1.

Formal charge = valence electrons - (lone pair electrons + ½ bonding electrons). Nitrogen has 5 valence electrons. In the described structure, N has no lone pairs, one double bond (4 bonding electrons), and two single bonds (4 bonding electrons), for 8 bonding electrons total. Thus FC = 5 - (0 + 8/2) = 5 - 4 = +1.

The formal charge is calculated as: Formal Charge = (valence electrons) − (non-bonding electrons) − 1/2(bonding electrons). Carbon belongs to group 14 and has 4 valence electrons. In the given structure of CO (:C≡O:), the carbon atom has one lone pair (2 non-bonding electrons) and shares a triple bond (6 bonding electrons). Therefore, Formal Charge(C) = 4 − 2 − (6 / 2) = 4 − 2 − 3 = −1.

Carbon has 4 valence electrons. In the described Lewis structure, C has one lone pair (2 electrons) and is in a triple bond, so it shares 6 bonding electrons. Formal charge = valence electrons − (lone-pair electrons + ½ bonding electrons) = 4 − (2 + 3) = −1.

Xenon (Xe) has 8 valence electrons. In XeF₄, it forms four single covalent bonds with fluorine atoms, using 4 electrons. The remaining 4 valence electrons form 2 lone pairs on the central xenon atom. With 4 bonding pairs and 2 lone pairs, the steric number is 6, giving an octahedral electron-pair geometry. To minimize electron repulsion, the two lone pairs occupy trans (opposite) positions, resulting in a square planar molecular geometry.

Xenon in XeF₄ has 8 valence electrons. Four fluorine atoms form four Xe–F single bonds, using 4 electrons, leaving 4 electrons as two lone pairs on Xe. There are therefore 6 electron domains around xenon: 4 bonding pairs and 2 lone pairs. Six electron domains give an octahedral electron-pair arrangement. The two lone pairs occupy opposite positions in the octahedron to minimize repulsion, so the molecular shape of the atoms is square planar.

Bromine (Br) has 7 valence electrons. In BrF₃, it forms three single covalent bonds with fluorine atoms, using 3 electrons, leaving 4 non-bonding electrons which constitute 2 lone pairs. The steric number (number of electron domains) around the central Br atom is 3 bonding pairs + 2 lone pairs = 5. A steric number of 5 corresponds to a trigonal bipyramidal arrangement of electron pairs (electron-domain geometry). To minimize electron-electron repulsion, the two lone pairs occupy equatorial positions, resulting in a T-shaped molecular geometry.

Bromine in BrF3 has 7 valence electrons, and each of the three fluorine atoms contributes one electron for bonding, giving (7 + 3)/2 = 5 electron pairs around Br. There are 3 bonding pairs and 2 lone pairs. Five electron pairs arrange in a trigonal bipyramidal electron-pair geometry. The two lone pairs occupy equatorial positions to minimize repulsions, leaving one equatorial and two axial fluorine atoms. This gives a T-shaped molecular geometry.

A central atom with six electron domains adopts an octahedral electron-pair geometry. For the molecular geometry to be square pyramidal, there must be 5 bonding domains (attached atoms) and 1 lone pair on the central atom. Checking the options:
- SF₆ has 6 single bonds and 0 lone pairs (octahedral).
- XeF₄ has 4 single bonds and 2 lone pairs (square planar).
- PCl₅ has 5 single bonds and 0 lone pairs (trigonal bipyramidal, 5 domains).
- IF₅ has 7 valence electrons on iodine; 5 form bonds with fluorine atoms, leaving 1 nonbonding electron pair (5 bonding pairs + 1 lone pair = 6 domains, square pyramidal shape).

Average particle speed is inversely proportional to the square root of the molar mass (v_rms = sqrt(3RT/M)). At 400 K, all gases share the same temperature and average kinetic energy per mole. The molar masses are approximately 20.18 g/mol for Ne, 28.02 g/mol for N₂, and 70.90 g/mol for Cl₂. Since Ne has the smallest molar mass, it has the highest average speed, followed by N₂, and then Cl₂. Thus, the order from greatest to least speed is Ne > N₂ > Cl₂.

Six electron domains give an octahedral electron-pair geometry. A square pyramidal molecular shape occurs when five positions are bonded atoms and one position is a lone pair, i.e., AX5E. IF5 has iodine with 5 bonding pairs to F and 1 lone pair, totaling 6 electron domains, so it is square pyramidal. SF6 is octahedral (6 bonds, no lone pair). XeF4 has 6 domains but 2 lone pairs, giving square planar. PCl5 has only 5 electron domains.

At the same temperature, all gases have the same average translational kinetic energy per particle: KE_avg = (1/2)mv_rms² = (3/2)kT. Solving gives v_rms = √(3RT/M), and average speed is proportional to 1/√M. Therefore, the gas with the smallest molar mass has the greatest average speed. Molar masses are approximately Ne: 20.18 g/mol, N₂: 28.02 g/mol, and Cl₂: 70.90 g/mol. Thus the ranking from greatest to least average particle speed is Ne > N₂ > Cl₂.

object.final_answer: A network solid, such as silicon carbide
object.working: Metallic solids conduct electricity in both solid and liquid states. Molecular solids typically have low melting points and are soft. Ionic solids have high melting points and are brittle, but they conduct electricity when molten due to the presence of mobile ions. Network covalent solids (like silicon carbide, SiC) are very hard and brittle, have extremely high melting points (above 1,700°C), and do not conduct electricity in either the solid or liquid state because they lack free electrons or mobile ions. Thus, the solid is a network covalent solid.

object.final_answer: An ionic solid, such as sodium chloride
object.working: Ionic solids are characterized by brittleness (shattering under stress due to repulsion between like charges when layers shift), high melting points (801°C is specifically the melting point of NaCl), lack of electrical conductivity in the solid state due to fixed ions, and good electrical conductivity in the molten state because ions become mobile charge carriers. Metallic solids conduct as solids and are malleable. Covalent network solids typically have much higher melting points and do not conduct when melted. Molecular solids have low melting points and do not conduct when melted.

object.final_answer: A network solid, such as silicon carbide
object.working: The sample is very hard, brittle, and has a very high melting point, which rules out molecular solids like CO2. It does not conduct as a solid or when molten. Metallic solids conduct in both states, so tungsten is not a match. Ionic solids like MgO are hard, brittle, and high-melting, but they conduct electricity when molten because ions become mobile. Therefore the sample is most likely a network covalent solid such as silicon carbide, which is very hard, high-melting, and nonconducting in both solid and molten states.

object.final_answer: An ionic solid, such as sodium chloride
object.working: The properties match an ionic solid. Ionic solids are brittle and shatter when struck because like-charged ions can be forced into alignment, causing repulsion. They have high melting points due to strong electrostatic attractions; NaCl melts at 801°C. In the solid state, ions are fixed in the lattice and cannot move, so the solid does not conduct electricity. When melted, the ions are free to move, so the molten ionic compound conducts electricity well. Metallic solids conduct as solids and are malleable, covalent network solids are extremely hard and generally do not conduct when melted, and molecular solids have much lower melting points.

object.final_answer: A molecular solid, such as solid sulfur
object.working: Molecular solids are held together by relatively weak intermolecular forces (such as London dispersion forces). Consequently, they typically have low melting points (119°C is relatively low), are soft, do not conduct electricity in either solid or molten states (no free mobile ions or electrons), and nonpolar molecular solids dissolve readily in nonpolar solvents. Octasulfur (S8) is a classic example: it is a yellow, soft molecular solid with a melting point near 115–119°C. In contrast, ionic solids have high melting points and conduct when melted; covalent network solids have very high melting points and are very hard; metallic solids conduct electricity in both solid and liquid states.

object.final_answer: A molecular solid, such as solid sulfur
object.working: The solid is soft, has a relatively low melting point (119°C), dissolves in nonpolar solvents, and does not conduct electricity in either solid or liquid state. These are characteristic properties of molecular solids, which consist of discrete molecules held by weak intermolecular forces. Solid sulfur is a yellow molecular solid with a low melting point and is soluble in nonpolar solvents. Ionic solids are hard, high-melting, and conduct when molten. Covalent network solids are very hard and high-melting. Metallic solids conduct electricity as solids and liquids.

object.final_answer: Warmer CO₂ molecules have greater average kinetic energy, so more of them overcome their weak attractions to water molecules and escape from the solution into the gas phase.
object.working: The dissolution of a gas in water is generally an exothermic process. As temperature increases, the average kinetic energy of the dissolved solute molecules increases. This allows a larger fraction of the CO₂ molecules to overcome the intermolecular attractions (dipole-induced dipole and dispersion forces) between the CO₂ and water molecules, shifting the dynamic equilibrium toward the gas phase and decreasing the solubility of the gas.

object.final_answer: Warmer CO₂ molecules have greater average kinetic energy, so more of them overcome their weak attractions to water molecules and escape from the solution into the gas phase.
object.working: The solubility of a gas in a liquid decreases as temperature increases. At higher temperature, dissolved CO₂ molecules have greater average kinetic energy. More of them can overcome the intermolecular attractions holding them in solution and escape into the gas phase, so the warm soda loses CO₂ faster and becomes flatter. Choice A is wrong because warmer water has weaker, not stronger, hydrogen bonding. Choice C is wrong because these temperatures do not decompose CO₂. Choice D is wrong because CO₂ solubility does depend on temperature, not only on water evaporation.

object.final_answer: A single X-ray photon carries far more energy than a single microwave photon, because its far shorter wavelength means a far greater frequency (c = λν) and E = hν.
object.working: The energy of an individual photon depends solely on its frequency (or wavelength), according to E = hν = hc/λ. Shorter wavelengths correspond to higher frequencies and thus higher photon energies. An X-ray photon (λ ≈ 0.1 nm = 10⁻¹⁰ m) has a much shorter wavelength and higher frequency than a microwave photon (λ ≈ 0.12 m), giving it far greater energy per photon. Total beam intensity reflects the total number of photons delivered per unit time multiplied by individual photon energy, which does not alter single-photon energy. Additionally, all electromagnetic waves travel at the same speed c in a vacuum.

object.final_answer: A single X-ray photon carries far more energy than a single microwave photon, because its far shorter wavelength means a far greater frequency (c = λν) and E = hν.
object.working: Photon energy is E = hν = hc/λ. For X-rays, λ ≈ 0.1 nm = 1 × 10^-10 m. For microwaves, λ ≈ 12 cm = 0.12 m. The energy ratio is E_X-ray / E_microwave = λ_microwave / λ_X-ray = 0.12 / (1 × 10^-10) ≈ 1.2 × 10^9, so a single X-ray photon is about a billion times more energetic than a single microwave photon. Intensity describes total energy delivered per second and does not determine energy per photon. All electromagnetic radiation travels at speed c in a vacuum.
